outline.guidance: Open with a 40–60 word direct answer paragraph structured for AI extraction: define SLS sensitivity toothpaste as a toothpaste formulated without sodium lauryl sulfate, specifically for people whose mouths react to SLS with canker sores, peeling tissue, or general irritation. Then in 2–3 sentences expand on why this matters — SLS is in the majority of conventional toothpastes, and sensitive mouths often suffer silently without knowing the cause. End with a brief road map sentence telling readers what this post covers. Do not use a question as the opening sentence. Do not mention competitor brand names.

outline.section: H2: What Is SLS and Why Does It Cause Sensitivity?
outline.guidance: Explain what sodium lauryl sulfate is: a synthetic surfactant added to toothpaste primarily to create foam. Clarify that its foaming action is cosmetic — it does not improve cleaning efficacy. Then explain the sensitivity mechanism: SLS strips away the protective mucosal lining of the mouth (the epithelium), which can expose underlying tissue to irritants, trigger canker sores (recurrent aphthous ulcers), cause tissue peeling, and heighten general oral sensitivity. Cite at least one external peer-reviewed source here — a good candidate is the study by Healy et al. (2000) in the Journal of Oral Pathology & Medicine linking SLS toothpaste to canker sore frequency, or the NIH/PubMed database. Use hyperlinked anchor text for the citation (e.g., 'research published in the Journal of Oral Pathology & Medicine'), not a bare URL. Distinguish between true SLS allergy and SLS sensitivity/intolerance — both warrant switching. Do not mention competitor brand names.

outline.section: H2: Signs You May Have SLS Sensitivity
outline.guidance: Use a short bulleted list (5–7 items) of common signs that SLS in toothpaste may be causing problems: recurring canker sores or mouth ulcers, peeling or sloughing of inner cheek tissue, burning sensation when brushing, general oral soreness that improves when toothpaste use is skipped, taste disturbances (SLS is known to temporarily suppress sweetness receptors, making food taste bitter), and dry or irritated lips. After the list, add 2–3 sentences of context: note that these symptoms often go undiagnosed because people don't associate them with toothpaste, and that switching to an SLS-free toothpaste is typically the first recommended step. Keep tone empathetic and practical.

outline.section: H2: What to Look for in a Toothpaste for SLS Sensitivity
outline.guidance: This section educates on how to read a toothpaste label to find SLS and its variants (also listed as sodium dodecyl sulfate, sodium laurilsulfate — confirm exact INCI aliases before writing). Then outline the key attributes of a genuinely good toothpaste for sensitive mouths: (1) SLS-free formula — the baseline requirement; (2) gentle abrasive system — avoid high-RDA abrasives; (3) soothing or remineralizing active ingredients such as nano hydroxyapatite or baking soda, which support enamel and gum health without irritation; (4) free from artificial dyes, synthetic flavors, and other common irritants; (5) fluoride or fluoride-free depending on preference — acknowledge both camps exist without being prescriptive. Briefly explain hydroxyapatite toothpaste as a fluoride-free remineralization alternative gaining clinical support. Do not recommend specific competitor products. Naturally weave in Real Skin Care's toothpaste formulation attributes (fluoride-free, SLS-free) as an example of what this looks like in practice.

outline.guidance: This is the brand-positioning section. Describe Real Skin Care's SLS-free toothpaste here by name, referencing its actual formula attributes (fluoride-free, SLS-free — confirmed per standing instructions). Do not fabricate or assume additional ingredients; stick to what is confirmed. Write this as an editorial recommendation, not a product description. Link naturally to the Real Skin Care SLS-free toothpaste collection page. Frame the recommendation around the reader's need: 'If you're dealing with SLS sensitivity, switching to a formula like [product] eliminates the primary irritant while still delivering a clean, fresh result.' Keep tone confident and direct.

outline.section: H2: Frequently Asked Questions About SLS Sensitivity and Toothpaste
outline.guidance: Include 4–5 FAQ items formatted with H3 sub-questions. Suggested questions (writer may refine for naturalness): (1) 'Is SLS in toothpaste safe?' — answer: for most people yes, but for those with sensitivity it causes real oral tissue disruption; cite the mucosal mechanism briefly. (2) 'What is the difference between SLS sensitivity and a toothpaste allergy?' — sensitivity is a dose-dependent irritant response; allergy is an immune-mediated reaction; both justify switching. (3) 'Can SLS toothpaste cause canker sores?' — yes, multiple studies suggest a link; reference the same citation used earlier. (4) 'Is fluoride-free toothpaste okay for sensitive teeth?' — explain hydroxyapatite as a remineralizing alternative; acknowledge that fluoride preference is personal and both options exist SLS-free. (5) 'How quickly will symptoms improve after switching to SLS-free toothpaste?' — typically within 1–3 weeks as oral mucosa regenerates, though individual results vary. Each answer should be 40–60 words — concise and AI-extractable. Apply FAQPage schema to this section.

Natural formulas that skip SLS and other synthetic irritants are the most effective choice for sensitive mouths.
